2.text: with his fur shirt on, and of course the knife had abundant room to slide

3.text: under his arm between the ample folds of the fur garment.

4.text: Scratching-Woman, however, offered to stab himself on the bare body.

5.text: For this purpose he obliged me to give him a new knife, which, after the

6.text: feast, was to become his property and to be used in magic medicine. The

7.text: knife must be keen-edged and sharp-pointed. Then Scratching-Woman started

8.text: beating the drum, in order, according to his explanation, to “heat” the knife

9.text: and to warm his body to a degree at which stabbing becomes harmless. He

10.text: explained naïvely that the performance with the shirt on might be executed
10.note: §2.15 withdrawn: printed mark restored, read off the scan

11.text: without “heating” the knife. The women of his household, however, protested

12.text: violently all the time against the performance. They even reproached me

13.text: with wanting to shorten the shaman’s life, because, according to their words,

14.text: feats like this, even when ending without immediate harm, are nevertheless

15.text: highly destructive to the vital forces of the shaman.

16.text: At last, when Scratching-Woman was almost ready to proceed with his

17.text: experiment, and beat the drum for the last time, there suddenly appeared

18.text: on the scene a “separate voice,” which claimed to belong to a female “spirit”

19.text: among the acquaintances of Scratching-Woman. This new party declared that,

20.text: Scratching-Woman, conformably to a promise given a year ago, owed her a

21.text: sacrifice of a reindeer, and she requested her due, forbidding the performance

22.text: of any shamanistic feats till after the liquidation of the debt.

23.text: Since it was summer-time, and the herds were away from the houses

24.text: and would join them only in the fall, the interdiction by the female “spirit”

25.text: put the whole matter of stabbing out of the question. Scratching-Woman,

26.text: however, did not wish me to think he was merely boasting of his exploits,

27.text: and, to prove his veracity, he showed me two deep scars on his abdomen,

28.text: one of which, he asserted, was produced by the knife, and the other by a

29.text: bullet from a rifle in a tour de force like those described.

30.text: In tales and other relations of a similar kind, the exploit of stabbing

31.text: one’s self with a knife is one of the most common achievements of the

32.text: shamanistic art, and it is so generally practised that the spectators are

33.text: said to ascribe little importance to it. A wooden imitation of a knife is

34.text: said to be often used, which evidently makes the simulation still more

35.text: apparent. Thus the account of a family feud¹ makes mention of a young

36.text: shaman-girl, a “woman able to stab herself” with impunity. This ability,

37.text: however, did not prevent her being murdered.

38.text: A tale collected among the Chukchee of the Anui mentions two rival

39.text: wives of one man. One of them, who had been driven from her home,

40.text: succeeded in going back with many rich peltries obtained by supernatural aid

41.text: and by the protection of a great black bear. The other was skilful in stabbing
